summaries.example: Think about a stack of building blocks. You can explain the shape of a small tower by looking at the blocks that make it up. Philosophers ask whether reality is like this: does everything depend on some most basic things, or could the explaining continue forever? They also ask whether the basic things must be independent, or whether they could depend on one another in a loop.
summaries.summary: Fundamentality is a philosophical idea about what is basic in reality. Philosophers ask whether some things are independent, whether a smallest group of things can account for everything else, or whether “fundamental” is simply a basic feature that cannot be defined using something deeper. They also disagree about the shape of dependence. It might end at a foundation, continue forever, or form a circle. The idea can apply to objects, properties, and facts. It is related to science because scientists often look for basic parts of nature, but metaphysicians are asking a broader question about reality as a whole.
key_ideas: Philosophers use “fundamental” to ask what is most basic in reality.
One approach says that fundamental things are independent in a chosen sense.
Another approach says that fundamental things form a complete, minimal basis for everything else.
Some philosophers allow dependence to continue forever or to form loops instead of ending at a foundation.
What counts as fundamental may concern objects, properties, or facts.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps philosophers think about explanation. If one thing depends on another, what explains the second thing? A theory of fundamentality tries to describe where explanations begin, whether they need to begin at all, and how different parts or levels of reality fit together. These questions can also affect how we understand science and the relationship between everyday things and their smaller parts.

important_terms.definition: The idea that something is basic, rather than depending on something deeper or more basic.
A connection in which one thing relies on another for its being or explanation.
A basic thing or fact that does not need another thing of the relevant kind to explain it.
The view that reality has some foundation that fully accounts for everything else.
The view that dependence might continue forever, without reaching a final foundation.

questions_to_think_about: Must every explanation eventually reach something basic?
Could a complete explanation contain many basic things rather than just one?
Can something be basic in one way but dependent in another way?
Would a loop of explanations really explain anything?

summaries.example: Suppose a theory says that a city is fully described by a complete account of its physical microstructure. The microstructural facts might be treated as a minimal complete basis: remove some of them and the city is no longer fully accounted for. But this does not automatically show that the microstructural facts are ungrounded. They might be fundamental in the sense of belonging to a complete basis while still standing in another dependence relation. This illustrates why independence and completeness can come apart.
summaries.summary: The metaphysical notion of fundamentality concerns what is basic in reality, but the source emphasizes that there may be several legitimate ways to understand “basic.” Independence-based accounts define fundamental entities by the absence of relevant dependence. Absolute independence considers every relevant dependence relation and is therefore extremely demanding; restricted independence considers only selected relations, often grounding or mereological dependence. A different approach describes fundamental entities as a complete minimal basis: together they account for everything else, while no smaller group does so. Primitivism denies that fundamentality can be defined in more basic terms, though it can still be characterized by its role in an overall theory. These accounts connect to larger disputes. Foundationalists hold that reality has a foundation, while infinitists allow some forms of endless descent. Coherentists allow dependence loops or mutual dependence. The source also warns that well-foundedness, completeness, and independence are not interchangeable, especially when infinite structures are considered.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes two central jobs for fundamentality: identifying an independent foundation and identifying a complete basis for everything else.
Absolute independence requires independence from every relevant metaphysical dependence relation, making it an exceptionally strong proposal.
Restricted independence selects one or more dependence relations, so an entity can be fundamental relative to grounding, parthood, or another chosen relation.
A complete minimal basis emphasizes coverage and minimality rather than simply being ungrounded.
Primitivism treats fundamentality as basic rather than definable, raising questions about how we can identify fundamental entities.
Foundationalism, infinitism, and coherentism offer different pictures: dependence may terminate, continue without a final base, or form cycles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fundamentality is meant to clarify the structure of reality and the direction of explanation. It can help express why one level of description might depend on another—for example, why biological facts might depend on chemical facts, which might depend on physical facts. But the debate also tests whether “the fundamental level” is a single thing, a plurality, an independently defined notion, or even a misleading picture. Distinguishing metaphysical fundamentality from fundamentality in physics prevents scientific claims and metaphysical claims from being treated as automatically identical.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical status of being basic or primitive in reality; the entry examines several competing ways to characterize it.
A relation in which one entity, fact, or property relies on another for its being, structure, or explanation.
A non-causal “in virtue of” relation often used to describe what explains or accounts for something at a metaphysical level.
A definition on which something is fundamental only relative to selected dependence relations, such as grounding or parthood.
A group of entities that is sufficient to determine or completely describe everything else, with no proper subgroup having that same role.
The position that fundamentality cannot be defined in more basic terms, although it may be characterized and assessed within a wider theory.
The thesis that every non-fundamental entity is fully accounted for by fundamental entities, in a suitably specified dependence relation.
The rejection of metaphysical foundationalism; in stronger forms, dependence never reaches a complete foundation.

questions_to_think_about: Which dependence relations should count when defining fundamentality, and why those rather than others?
Can a complete basis exist even if none of its members is absolutely independent?
Does an infinite chain need a final foundation to provide an adequate explanation?
If grounding can be mutual or circular, can reality still have a hierarchy?
Should physical fundamentality and metaphysical fundamentality be treated as the same issue?

summaries.example: Imagine a school play. The final performance depends on many things: the script, actors, costumes, and stage. One person might say the actors are most basic because the play cannot happen without them. Another might say the complete set of script, actors, costumes, and stage is the smallest group that accounts for the performance. A third might say each part depends on the others in a complicated way. Philosophers use similar questions when asking what reality depends on.
summaries.summary: Fundamentality asks what, if anything, is basic in reality. The question is not limited to tiny physical particles: philosophers may discuss objects, properties, or facts. One family of views connects fundamentality with independence. Absolute independence requires freedom from every relevant kind of metaphysical dependence, while restricted independence chooses only certain relations, such as grounding or dependence on parts. Another family focuses on a complete minimal basis, a smallest group that determines or fully describes everything else. Primitivism takes fundamentality as a basic feature that cannot be defined in simpler terms. These proposals lead to disagreements about the overall structure of reality. Metaphysical foundationalism says dependence has a foundation. Metaphysical infinitism says some dependence may continue endlessly. Metaphysical coherentism allows cycles in which entities depend on one another. The source also explains that an infinite chain need not always be a simple failure: some infinite structures might still have a kind of completeness or foundation.
key_ideas: Fundamentality can concern objects, properties, or facts, depending on the philosophical theory.
Absolute independence is very strong because it requires independence from all relevant dependence relations.
Restricted independence is more flexible because it focuses on selected relations, such as grounding or part-whole dependence.
The complete-minimal-basis approach asks whether a smallest group can account for all of reality.
Philosophers disagree about whether dependence must end, may continue forever, or can form loops.
The metaphysical use of “fundamental” is broader than asking which physical theory is most basic.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often assume that explanations must eventually reach a bottom level. Fundamentality makes that assumption explicit and asks whether it is justified. The debate matters for understanding how different sciences and levels of description relate, but metaphysical fundamentality should not simply be identified with whatever physics currently calls basic. It also matters because different accounts can change what counts as a satisfactory explanation of the world.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical idea of what is most basic or deepest in reality.
Relying on something else in a way that is not merely a matter of timing or physical cause.
A relation expressed by saying that one fact or thing holds “in virtue of” another.
Being independent with respect to one or more chosen kinds of dependence, rather than every possible kind.
A smallest collection of entities that together accounts for everything else.
The view that the fundamental level cannot be defined using a more basic idea.
The view that dependence eventually has a foundation made of fundamental entities or facts.
The view that dependence may go on without reaching a final foundation.

questions_to_think_about: If something is independent as a part, could it still depend on something in another way?
Is a smallest complete basis guaranteed to be unique?
Would an endless chain of explanations be a failure, or could it still explain things?
Can circular dependence provide understanding, or does explanation require a one-way order?
What evidence, if any, could support a theory about what is fundamental?
